content: The patient monitoring systems assessment checklist is a tool designed to evaluate the presence and quality of various components essential for effective patient monitoring. This checklist should be tailored to the specific healthcare setting and utilized at the start of each annual patient monitoring review visit. It provides a structured review of the following key areas: 1. Integrated Systems and National Tools: Assess whether patient monitoring systems for HIV, MNCH/HIV, and TB/HIV are integrated. Determine if HIV patient monitoring tools are utilized in the MNCH setting and list all applicable tools. Evaluate whether TB patient monitoring tools are used in the MNCH setting and list them. Confirm if MNCH patient monitoring tools include HIV-related elements, such as ANC/maternal health cards, ANC registers, labor records, L&D registers, child health cards, or other specified tools. Check if there is a separate patient record for HIV-exposed infants and whether an HIV-exposed infant or mother–infant pair register exists. Verify if the HIV-exposed infant or mother–infant pair register is linked to the ANC or ART register entries for the mother. Assess whether HIV patient monitoring tools are used in TB clinics and list them. Consider integration with other programs, such as hepatitis or non-communicable diseases (e.g., hypertension, diabetes), as appropriate. 2. Human Resource Capacity: Confirm that all relevant staff in HIV clinics have received appropriate training on the national patient monitoring system within the past specified months. Identify the number of trained doctors, nurses, data clerks, lay counselors, and other staff, and specify their training on cards, registers, reports, and data use. Ensure that relevant HIV staff are trained in the use of TB patient monitoring tools. If staff are not adequately trained, the district team should schedule and provide training or retraining, followed by hands-on support within 2–4 weeks. 3. Availability of National Patient Monitoring Tools: Verify that national patient monitoring tools, such as patient-held cards, HIV patient cards, community ART monitoring tools, ART registers, cross-sectional reports, ART cohort analysis reports, appointment books, and transfer/referral forms, are available in adequate supply. If tools are missing or in short supply, the district team should ensure their availability by providing new forms or copies to the facility. Confirm that the facility team has recently received training in patient monitoring. 4. Use of Patient Monitoring Tools: Confirm that the facility is using national patient monitoring tools. If additional or alternative tools are being used, list them and provide reasons for their use. Ensure that any non-MoH tools or forms implemented by donors or other institutions are authorized by the MoH and do not duplicate national tools. Minimize the use of additional tools wherever possible. 5. Organization and Storage of Patient Monitoring Tools: Ensure that HIV patient cards and ART registers are well-organized and stored securely. Verify that unique patient IDs are generated systematically according to national standards and provided to each patient enrolled in HIV care. Address any issues with disorganized or insecure records by providing adequate space, shelving, or locked storage with limited access. 6. Patient and Data Flow: Confirm that HIV patient cards are pulled from storage for all patients to be seen at the start of the day, follow patients through care, and are returned to registration after each visit. If patient cards are not updated or do not follow patients, discuss with the facility team to understand and address data flow issues. Use flow diagrams if necessary to improve understanding and efficiency. 7. Completeness and Accuracy of HIV Patient Cards: Take a sample of five HIV patient cards and check for completeness and accuracy in various sections, including sociodemographic information, family status, HIV care summary, prior ARVs, ART care, treatment interruptions, follow-up status, and encounter pages. Ensure that relevant information, such as TB status, weight, pregnancy status, and nutritional data for infants, is recorded at each visit. Address any gaps or errors by discussing them with the responsible health worker and providing additional training or support as needed. 8. ART Register Validation: Ensure that ART registers are filled in following the start of ART and updated with each patient visit. Verify that columns are completed using standardized coding and that patient information is organized systematically. Validate ART cohort reports using ART registers and re-tally columns to ensure accuracy. If the facility is unable to complete the ART cohort report, the district team should assist during site visits. 9. Appointment System: Confirm that an appointment book or system is used to log patients’ next visits, prepare clinic days, identify missed appointments, and follow up with patients who miss appointments. Ensure that patient and treatment supporter contact information is updated and complete. Record dates for lost-to-follow-up (LTF) patients on summary forms. 10. Transfer/Referral System: Verify that standard transfer forms are used to receive and transfer patients and that health centers follow national transfer protocols. If no transfer protocol exists, ensure that key information, such as sociodemographic characteristics and treatment summaries, is transferred with the patient. 11. Data Use: Confirm that health workers hold regular meetings to review patient charts or conduct case management reviews. Ensure that health workers understand how to use information on patient cards and registers to manage patient care and treatment effectively. Address any gaps in understanding or training by providing additional support and follow-up. For each of these areas, any identified gaps or deficiencies should be addressed promptly through recommended actions, including training, resource provision, and system improvements. Follow-up plans should be developed to ensure ongoing compliance and effectiveness.
